title: Random Forest
summary: Why a random forest beats one deep tree: averaging unstable trees cuts variance, and random feature subsets lower the correlation that sets the floor averaging can't get below.
objectives: **Explain** why deep decision trees are the ideal thing to average (unstable, low-bias, high-variance) and why bagging barely helps stable learners like k-NN
**Compute** the variance of an average of B correlated trees, `ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B`, and say which term more trees remove and which only lower correlation removes
**Explain** how random feature subsets per split (`max_features`) lower tree correlation when a few strong features dominate, and why too small a subset hurts
**Describe** how out-of-bag error is formed (~37% of rows left out per tree) and why it is a held-out estimate
**Map** the theory onto scikit-learn knobs: `max_features`, `n_estimators`, depth/leaf size, `oob_score`, and the impurity-vs-permutation importance caveat

steps.title: One juror is shaky
steps.narration: Picture a single juror who is decent but erratic. Hear the case a little differently, with two facts shifted, and the verdict flips. A good judge on average, but you can't trust any one verdict. Some predictors behave exactly like this: small changes to what they learn from change their answer a lot [S3].

steps.title: Many jurors, independent mistakes

state.caption: Each juror errs on their own

steps.narration: Now seat nine such jurors. Each still makes mistakes, but **their own** mistakes, scattered in different places. Three are wrong, six are right, and the majority lands on the right verdict. A crowd of independent, better-than-chance voters is far more reliable than any one of them [S7].

steps.title: Same newspaper, same mistakes
steps.narration: Now every juror read the same newspaper before the trial. When the paper is misleading, they all get it wrong **together**. Nine copies of one mistake is no better than one juror. Forests hit this exact problem when one strong clue dominates every member [S8].

callout.text: Agreement isn't the goal; independent errors are.

whatChanged: - the majority now fails with them

steps.title: Give each juror different evidence

state.caption: Different slices of evidence, independent mistakes

steps.narration: Hand each juror a different random slice of the evidence for each question. Their mistakes scatter again and the majority recovers. That is a **random forest**: jurors are decision trees, and the slices are random rows (a **bootstrap** sample) plus random features at each split [S7] [S2].

callout.text: Where it breaks: jurors with too little evidence each get worse, so there is a sweet spot (see the Technical tab).

whatChanged: + each juror gets a different slice

steps.title: One deep tree is unstable
steps.narration: A deep tree fits its training data closely, so its **bias** is low. But change two rows and it can grow a different shape, even a different root split, so its **variance** is high [S2]. Breiman calls this instability the vital element: it is what makes averaging worth doing [S3].

steps.title: Draw a bootstrap sample
steps.narration: To get a different tree from the same data, draw a **bootstrap sample**: pick N rows *with replacement*. Some rows land in the bag twice or three times; others never get picked. Each bag is a slightly different version of the training set [S3].

steps.title: About 37% sit out
steps.narration: The rows that were never drawn sit this tree out. On average a bootstrap sample leaves out about **37%** of the rows, roughly a third [S11]. These are the tree's **out-of-bag** (OOB) rows: data it never saw, ready to test it on. Here 4 of 12 sit out.

callout.text: Each row is out of bag for roughly a third of the trees. That's a free validation set [S2].

steps.title: Grow many trees, average them
steps.narration: Grow one deep tree per bag, then average their outputs (regression) or take a vote (classification). This is **bagging**. In Breiman's tests it cut classification-tree error by 20% to 47% [S3]. Averaging attacks the **variance** term of the error [S1], so the bar drops below a single tree's.

steps.title: But the trees look alike
steps.narration: Look at the roots. One strong feature, D, wins the top split in nearly every bagged tree, so the trees make similar predictions: they are **correlated**, and averaging correlated trees helps less [S8]. The overlap between bags is not the main issue; the dominant feature is [S2].

callout.text: Breiman: the randomness has to minimise the correlation ρ while keeping the trees strong [S7].

steps.title: Random features at each split
steps.narration: Now each split may choose only from **m** randomly drawn features, typically m ≈ √p: here 3 of 9 [S2]. Feature D is missing for three of five roots, so those trees split on something else and grow differently. Correlation drops, and so does the variance of the average [S7].

steps.title: Variance = floor + shrinking part
steps.narration: For B trees with variance σ² and pairwise correlation ρ, the average has variance **ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B** [S5]. The dark part, ρσ², is a floor. The light part shrinks as you add trees. Bagging (ρ = 0.7) and the forest (ρ = 0.3) differ mostly in the floor.
whatChanged: ~ bar split into floor + shrinking part
+ bagging vs forest side by side

steps.title: Edge case: the floor and the trade-off
steps.narration: Jump to 1,000 trees. The light part all but vanishes, yet neither bar goes below its floor ρσ² [S5]. Pushing m down to 1 would lower ρ further, but each tree gets weaker [S9]. The randomness must cut correlation *while keeping strength* [S7].

callout.text: More trees ≠ zero variance. Only lower correlation lowers the floor.

code.title: Python (scikit-learn)
code.src:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

rf = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=500,      # set high; not a regulariser
    max_features="sqrt",   # m: the correlation-vs-strength knob
    min_samples_leaf=1,    # depth/leaf size: still regularises
    oob_score=True,        # free held-out estimate
    n_jobs=-1, random_state=0,
).fit(X_train, y_train)

print(rf.oob_score_)       # OOB accuracy
imp = permutation_importance(rf, X_val, y_val)  # not rf.feature_importances_

steps.title: The variance floor, in numbers
steps.narration: Take B identically distributed trees, each with variance σ², pairwise correlation ρ. Then Var = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B, which tends to **ρσ²** as B → ∞ [S5]. Worked example: σ² = 1, ρ = 0.5 gives a floor of 0.5, not 0. The infinite forest's variance is correlation times one tree's variance [S6].

callout.text: With ρ = 0.5 you can never get below half a tree's variance.

steps.title: Strength vs correlation
steps.narration: A tree's **margin** on a row is P(votes right) minus the largest P(votes for another class); **strength** s is the expected margin. Breiman bounds forest error by **ρ̄(1−s²)/s²**, with ρ̄ the mean correlation between trees: smaller ρ̄/s² is better [S7]. For regression, forest error ≤ ρ̄ × tree error [S7].

steps.title: max_features sweeps the trade-off
steps.narration: On the sonar data, strength stopped rising past about F = 4 while correlation kept climbing, so error dipped then rose [S7]. With 1,000 weak inputs, single trees had 60-80% error, yet the forest reached 2.8-10.7% against a 1.0% Bayes rate, because correlation stayed tiny [S7].

callout.text: Weak trees are fine if they're nearly uncorrelated.

steps.title: More trees converge; depth still matters
steps.narration: As trees are added, forest error converges almost surely to a limit, so more trees never overfit [S7]. For MSE and Brier score, more trees are never worse [S9]. But the limit depends on the trees: on low signal-to-noise data, shallower trees act as regularisation and do better [S10].

steps.title: Out-of-bag error
steps.narration: Each tree leaves out about 37% of rows, so each row gets roughly B/3 OOB votes [S11] [S2]. Predict every row using only those trees and you get the **OOB error**, about as accurate as a same-size test set [S7]. With few trees it runs slightly pessimistic, since each vote uses only a third of the forest [S7].

steps.title: sklearn defaults and importance
steps.narration: Defaults: 100 trees, `max_features="sqrt"`, unlimited depth, bootstrap on [S12]. The regressor's default 1.0 is plain bagging, and sklearn averages probabilities rather than counting votes [S4]. mtry is the knob most worth tuning [S9]. `feature_importances_` (MDI) favours high-cardinality features [S4]; prefer permutation importance: shuffle one feature, measure the error rise [S7].

callout.text: Two features carrying the same information each look important when permuted separately [S7].

quiz.q: Trees have variance σ² = 1 and pairwise correlation ρ = 0.3. As B → ∞, the variance of their average approaches…
quiz.why: Var = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B, and the second term vanishes, leaving ρσ² = 0.3 [S5].

quiz.q: Why do plain bagged trees stay correlated with each other?
options: Bootstrap samples share most of their rows
A few strong features win most top splits
Too few trees were grown for them to differ
Every tree is built with the same random seed
quiz.why: Strong predictors get chosen near the top of many bagged trees, making them alike; split-level feature sampling breaks this [S8] [S2].

quiz.q: Which part of Var = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B does lowering max_features target?
options: The ρσ² floor, by lowering ρ
σ², by making each tree stronger
quiz.why: A smaller max_features makes trees less correlated (lower ρ), at some cost in each tree's strength [S4] [S9].

quiz.q: With B = 100 trees, roughly how many out-of-bag predictions does each training row get?
quiz.why: Each bootstrap sample leaves out about 37% of rows, so with 100 trees a row is out of bag for about 37 of them [S11].

quiz.q: Past the point where strength plateaus, raising max_features further usually…
options: raises error, as correlation keeps rising
lowers error, as strength keeps growing
has no effect at all on the error
quiz.why: On the sonar data strength was flat past F ≈ 4 while correlation kept rising, and error rose [S7].

quiz.q: Bagging helps deep trees far more than k-NN because deep trees are…
options: unstable: small data changes reshape them
slow, and bagging runs them in parallel
shallow, so each one underfits the data
quiz.why: Breiman names instability as the vital element; k-nearest neighbours is stable, so bagging gains little [S3].

quiz.q: More trees don't overfit. What can still make a forest overfit noisy data?
quiz.why: Tree depth acts as regularisation: on low signal-to-noise data, shallower trees do better [S10].

quiz.q: In scikit-learn, RandomForestRegressor's default max_features=1.0 makes it…
quiz.why: max_features=1.0 considers every feature at every split, which is equivalent to bagged trees [S4].
